decks.title: Introduction — Part 1: Scarcity, Choice and Economic Activity
goals: Explain why scarcity of resources against unlimited wants forces choices
Describe consumption, production and distribution with examples
Identify consumers, producers, service holders and the government in a situation
Explain why economics needs numerical facts

slides.heading: Introduction: Why Economics Needs Numbers
slides.body_md: Part 1: **wants and scarcity**, **choice**, the **economic activities** and the **economic agents**.

visual.alt: Flow: unlimited wants meet limited resources, so choices have to be made, and economics studies these choices
visual.caption: The economic problem in four steps

slides.narration: Every day somebody decides how to use a limited sum of money, a limited amount of time or a limited piece of land. In this part we see why such choices arise, what economics studies, which three activities go on in every economy, and who the main actors are. Then we are ready to see why numbers are needed.

slides.heading: Unlimited wants, limited resources
slides.body_md: Human **wants are unlimited**: when one want is met, another appears. The **resources** that can satisfy them are **scarce** (limited) and can be put to **alternative uses**.

rows: Food, school fees, a phone, a holiday
Food and fees first; the holiday waits
Cakes and bread in the morning shift
Bread now, cakes in the afternoon
A road, a school room, a well

visual.alt: Table of three imagined cases of scarcity: a family with 10,000 rupees a month, a bakery with one oven, and a panchayat with one year of funds, each with wants, the limited resource and the choice made
visual.caption: In each case a want is postponed, which is the cost of choosing.

slides.narration: A family in Rangpur wants food, school fees, a phone and a holiday, but has only ten thousand rupees a month. A bakery has one oven. A panchayat has one year of funds. In each case something must wait. Wants are many and resources are few, and that gap is the heart of the economic problem.

slides.heading: Scarcity makes choice unavoidable
slides.body_md: Because resources are scarce and have alternative uses, every person and every society must **choose**.
bullets: Using a resource for one purpose means giving up another.
**Economics** is the study of how individuals and society **choose to use scarce resources** to satisfy their wants.
Rich or poor, every economy faces this problem.
slides.narration: Because resources are limited and can be used in different ways, choosing one use means giving up another. That is why we say economics is the study of how people and societies choose to use scarce resources to satisfy their wants. Even a very rich country has to choose, so the problem is never completely solved.

slides.heading: Quick check: wants and resources
slides.body_md: Which statement about wants and resources is correct?
slides.narration: Read all four statements. Ask whether wants or resources are the ones that never end, and whether choice can ever be avoided.

visual.caption: The three economic activities go on together in every economy.

slides.narration: Three activities go on in every economy. Production creates goods and services. Distribution shares the income of production among those who helped. Consumption uses goods to meet wants. The wants of consumers then create demand for more production, so the cycle keeps going.

slides.heading: Consumption, production and distribution
slides.body_md: **Consumption** uses goods and services to satisfy wants. **Production** creates them from inputs. **Distribution** shares the income of production as wages, rent, interest and profit.

rows: Using goods and services to satisfy wants
A family eats rice bought from the weekly market
Creating goods and services from inputs
A mill in Chandpur turns paddy into rice
Sharing the income of production among those who helped
The mill pays wages, rent and interest and keeps profit

visual.alt: Table defining consumption, production and distribution with an imagined example of each: a family eating rice, a mill turning paddy into rice, and the mill paying wages, rent and interest and keeping a profit

slides.narration: Consumption is using goods and services to meet wants, like a family eating rice. Production is creating goods and services, like a mill turning paddy into rice. Distribution is the sharing of the income earned in production, as wages to workers, rent to owners of land, interest to lenders and profit to the owner.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: name the activity
slides.body_md: Decide which activity each imagined event in the village of Chandpur shows.
bullets: Step 1: Is something new being **created**? That is production.
Step 2: Is income being **shared out** among those who helped? That is distribution.
Step 3: Is something being **used to meet a want**? That is consumption.
Step 4: Note that spending wages on rice is again consumption.

rows: The owner pays wages and keeps the profit
A household buys a water pot
A potter spends part of her wages on rice

visual.alt: Table of four imagined events in Chandpur and the economic activity each shows: shaping pots is production, paying wages and profit is distribution, and buying a pot or buying rice is consumption
visual.caption: One event can feed the next: wages are distributed, then spent.

slides.narration: Look at the events in Chandpur. Shaping pots from clay creates something new, so that is production. Paying wages and keeping profit shares the income, so that is distribution. A household buying a pot is consumption. A potter spending wages on rice is also consumption. One event leads to the next.

slides.heading: Quick check: harvest and use
slides.body_md: A farmer sells part of his wheat and keeps the rest for his own family. What is the family's eating of wheat?
slides.narration: Think about what is happening to the wheat the family keeps. Is anything new being made, is an income being shared, or is a want being met?

slides.heading: The economic agents
slides.body_md: The people and bodies who take economic decisions are **economic agents**: **consumers**, **producers**, **service holders** and the **government**.

rows: Uses goods and services to satisfy wants
Organises inputs and makes goods or services for sale
Earns a salary or wage by working for others
Rita teaching in a private school
Provides public services and raises revenue through taxes

visual.alt: Table of four economic agents, consumer, producer, service holder and government, with a meaning and an imagined example each

slides.narration: Four kinds of agents take economic decisions. Consumers use goods and services. Producers organise inputs and make goods for sale. Service holders earn a salary or wage by working for others. The government provides public services and raises revenue through taxes. One person can play more than one role, for example a teacher is both a service holder and a consumer.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: spot the agents
slides.body_md: In an imagined weaving unit in Chandpur, name the agent for each person or body.
bullets: Step 1: Who decides output and price? The owner, a **producer**.
Step 2: Who earns monthly wages? The weavers, **service holders**.
Step 3: Who buys the shawls? Households, **consumers**.
Step 4: Who collects tax? The **government**.

headers: Person or body in the weaving unit (imagined)
rows: The owner, who decides output and price
The tax office that collects the unit's tax

visual.alt: Table naming the agent for each person in an imagined weaving unit: the owner is a producer, weavers are service holders, households are consumers and the tax office is the government
visual.caption: One person can be more than one agent: a weaver also consumes.

slides.narration: In the weaving unit, the owner decides what to make and at what price, so the owner is a producer. The eight weavers earn monthly wages, so they are service holders. Households buy the shawls, so they are consumers. The tax office is part of the government. A weaver also consumes, so roles can overlap.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the agents
slides.body_md: Match each imagined person with the role in which she is acting.
slides.narration: For each person, ask what they are doing in this moment. Are they buying for own use, organising output, working for a salary, or providing a public service?

slides.heading: How the agents are linked

nodes.label: Producers make goods and pay wages

visual.alt: Flow showing how agents are linked: producers make goods and pay wages, service holders earn and spend, consumers buy goods, and the government taxes and provides services, which feeds back into production
visual.caption: The agents depend on one another

slides.narration: The agents depend on one another. Producers make goods and pay wages. Service holders earn and spend. Consumers buy the goods. The government taxes and provides services that producers and households use. Then the cycle repeats. Decisions at every point depend on facts about quantities and prices.

slides.heading: From choices to numbers
slides.body_md: Every choice rests on facts: how many, how much, how often. Economists need **numerical facts** and a method of handling them. That method is **statistics**.

visual.alt: Flow from an economic question to collecting numbers, summarising them, drawing a conclusion and making a decision
visual.caption: Decisions need facts; statistics supplies the method

slides.narration: To choose well, a farmer, a shopkeeper or a government needs facts. How much rain fell, how many buns were sold, how many households need ration shops. These are numbers. Collecting such numbers and drawing sound conclusions from them is the job of statistics, which we study in the second part.

slides.heading: Quick check: order the activities
slides.body_md: Arrange the events of the Karanpur cloth story in order.
slides.narration: Start with the event that creates something, then the event that shares the income, then the event that uses the goods.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Wants are unlimited and resources are scarce, so choice is unavoidable
The study of how individuals and society choose to use scarce resources

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the economic problem, economics, the three activities and the four agents

slides.narration: Wants are unlimited and resources are scarce, so choice is unavoidable. Economics studies how individuals and society choose. Consumption, production and distribution are the three activities. Consumers, producers, service holders and the government are the main agents. Their decisions depend on numerical facts.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define scarcity with **both** halves: unlimited wants and limited resources.
Do not mix **production** (creating) with **distribution** (sharing the income).
Name the agent from the **role played**, not from the person: a teacher earning a salary is a service holder.
Use a short, specific example for each activity and agent.
slides.narration: Always define scarcity with both halves: unlimited wants and limited resources. Do not confuse production, which is creating, with distribution, which is sharing income. Decide the agent from the role being played. Support each activity and agent with a short example. These habits earn marks.

Distinguish quantitative from qualitative data and summarise both
Explain the functions, uses and importance of statistics in economics
State the limitations of statistics and apply them to a claim

slides.heading: Statistics: Meaning, Uses and Limits
slides.body_md: Part 2: the **two senses** of statistics, **kinds of data**, **functions** and **limitations**.

visual.alt: Flow from an economic question to collecting numbers, summarising them, drawing a conclusion and making a decision
visual.caption: Decisions need facts; statistics supplies the method

slides.narration: In this part we meet statistics itself. We see the two ways the word is used, the two kinds of data, what statistics does for economics, who uses it, why it matters, and what it cannot do. Examples come from villages, shops and families.

slides.heading: Two senses of the word statistics
slides.body_md: In the **plural** sense, **statistics** means **numerical facts**, or data. In the **singular** sense, **statistics** is the **science** of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting data.

slides.narration: The word statistics is used in two senses. In the plural sense it means numerical facts, like six years of rainfall readings in a village. In the singular sense it means the science of dealing with such facts: collecting them, organising them, presenting them, analysing them and interpreting the results.

slides.heading: Five stages of statistics

visual.alt: Flow of the five stages of statistics as a science: collection, organisation, presentation, analysis and interpretation
visual.caption: Each stage builds on the previous one

slides.narration: Statistics as a science has five stages. First data are collected. Then they are organised, for example sorted into groups. Next they are presented in tables and diagrams. Then they are analysed, using measures like averages. Finally the results are interpreted, which means saying what they mean for the question.

slides.heading: Quick check: only collection?
slides.body_md: A student says statistics is only about collecting numbers. Which reply is correct?
slides.narration: Think of the five stages and decide which reply is complete.

slides.heading: Quantitative and qualitative data
slides.body_md: **Quantitative data** are measured as numbers, such as income or marks. **Qualitative data** are attributes, such as region or preference. Attributes can be **counted by category**.

visual.alt: Table comparing quantitative data, which are measured as numbers such as income, marks and rainfall, with qualitative data, which are attributes such as gender, region and preference and are summarised by counting categories

slides.narration: Quantitative data are measured as numbers, such as income, marks, price or rainfall. Qualitative data describe an attribute, such as gender, region or preference. You cannot measure an attribute, but you can count how many units fall in each category. Counting turns qualitative data into numbers.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sort the information
slides.body_md: In an imagined survey at the Lalpur canteen, decide the kind of data for each item.
bullets: Step 1: Can the item be **measured** in numbers? Pocket money, yes: quantitative.
Step 2: Is it an **attribute**? Favourite drink or class section: qualitative.
Step 3: A **count** of how many chose tea comes from a qualitative attribute.

rows: Pocket money of each student, in rupees

slides.narration: Look at the canteen survey. Pocket money in rupees is measured, so it is quantitative. Favourite drink and class section are attributes, so they are qualitative. The number of students who chose tea is a count obtained by sorting students into categories, so it summarises a qualitative attribute with a number.

Step 3: Farming: 32 ÷ 80 × 100 = 40 per cent.

slides.narration: Statistics does six jobs for economics. It presents facts precisely, it condenses large amounts of data, it finds relationships between economic factors, it helps in forecasting, it supports policy-making, and it helps test theories against real figures.

slides.heading: Presenting facts and condensing data
slides.body_md: **Precision:** exact figures replace loose remarks. **Condensing:** a mass of data is reduced to a few **summary measures**, such as an **average**.

visual.alt: Table of the imagined Kavita Provision Store sales over six days, 4,200, 3,800, 4,000, 4,600, 5,400, 5,000 rupees, total 27,000 and average 4,500
visual.caption: Six figures condensed into one: the average sale.

slides.narration: Instead of saying the village had good rain, a report can give exact readings. Instead of listing every day of sales, we can give the average. For the Kavita Provision Store, the six days add up to twenty seven thousand rupees, and the average is four thousand five hundred rupees a day. One figure now stands for six.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: price and quantity
slides.body_md: An imagined bakery records buns sold at different prices. Find the relationship.
bullets: Step 1: Place price and quantity side by side.
Step 2: Price rises from ₹10 to ₹18 and quantity falls from 50 to 26.
Step 3: Each ₹2 rise cuts sales by 6 buns.
Step 4: Price and quantity demanded move in **opposite** directions.

rows: Fall in buns sold for each ₹2 rise

visual.alt: Table of an imagined bakery: as the price of a bun rises from 10 to 18 rupees, buns sold per day fall from 50 to 26, a fall of 6 for each two rupee rise
visual.caption: Imagined bakery figures: price and quantity move in opposite directions.

slides.narration: Look at the bakery table. When the price of a bun rises from ten to twelve rupees, sales fall from fifty to forty four, a fall of six buns. Each further two rupee rise cuts sales by six more. Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions. Pairing the figures made this relationship visible.

slides.heading: Forecasting and policy-making
slides.body_md: Past data show a **trend**. A planner can use the trend to estimate the future need and to frame **policy**. A forecast is an estimate, not a guarantee.

visual.alt: Table of imagined rice consumption in Rangpur, 400, 420, 440, 460 tonnes a month in four years, rising by 20 tonnes each year, so the fifth year forecast is 480 tonnes
visual.caption: Imagined figures; the forecast assumes the trend continues.

slides.narration: Suppose monthly rice consumption in Rangpur was four hundred, four hundred twenty, four hundred forty and four hundred sixty tonnes in four years. It rises by twenty tonnes a year. If the trend continues, the next year needs about four hundred eighty tonnes, so stocks can be arranged in time. It is an estimate, and changes in conditions can make it wrong.

slides.heading: Who uses statistics, and why it matters
slides.body_md: **Consumers, producers, the government and researchers** use statistics. Economic **theories** are tested with data, and **policies** are framed and judged with data.

rows: Averaging asking prices of seven second-hand scooters
A bag maker studying sales in five towns
Matching ration shops to households in a block
Checking whether saving rises with income

visual.alt: Table of four users of statistics, consumer, producer, government and researcher, with what each uses it for and an imagined case

slides.narration: A buyer compares prices. A producer decides output and price. The government plans where to build facilities. A researcher checks whether saving rises with income. Theories are tested with data, and policies are framed and later judged with data, so statistics is important to every one of them.

slides.heading: A relationship in numbers: income and saving

visual.alt: Table of five imagined families: income 12, 18, 24, 30 and 36 thousand rupees; saving 1.2, 2.7, 4.8, 7.5 and 10.8 thousand; saving as a percentage of income 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30
visual.caption: Imagined figures: richer families here save a larger share.

slides.narration: Here are five imagined families. As income rises from twelve thousand to thirty six thousand rupees, saving rises from one point two thousand to ten point eight thousand. As a share of income, saving climbs from ten per cent to thirty per cent. Comparing paired figures is how economists study how two factors are related.

slides.heading: Limitations of statistics
slides.body_md: Statistics **deals with aggregates**, not single individuals. Its results are true **on the average**. It can be **misused** if data are collected or read carelessly.

rows: It describes groups, not a single unit
An average income of ₹36,000 says little about one family
A result need not hold in every case
Most richer families save more, but one may not
Careless data or reading gives wrong conclusions
Asking ten people at one counter and claiming all customers agree

visual.alt: Table of three limitations of statistics with a meaning and an imagined illustration each: it deals with aggregates, its results are true on the average, and it can be misused

slides.narration: Statistics has limits. It deals with groups, not single units, so an average income of thirty six thousand rupees does not tell us about one family. Its results are true on the average and need not hold in every case. And careless collection or reading of data can lead to wrong conclusions. These limits call for care, not for giving up statistics.

Give a **specific example** for each function.
For a percentage share, write the **formula** first and then substitute.
When asked to evaluate a claim, mention **aggregates** and **average truth**.
Do not say statistics is useless; say it must be used with care.

sections.heading: 1. Scarcity, choice and economics
sections.body_md:
Human **wants are unlimited**, but the **resources** that can satisfy them are **scarce** and have **alternative uses**. So individuals and societies must **choose**. **Economics** studies how they choose to use scarce resources to satisfy wants.

Example: an imagined family with ₹10,000 a month cannot buy everything; it puts food and school fees first and postpones a holiday.

key_terms.definition_md: The limited availability of resources compared with the wants they could satisfy.
The study of how individuals and society choose to use scarce resources to satisfy their wants.
The possibility of putting the same resource to different purposes.

sections.heading: 2. Economic activities and agents
sections.body_md:
**Consumption** is the use of goods and services to satisfy wants. **Production** is creating goods and services from inputs. **Distribution** is the sharing of the income of production among those who helped, as wages, rent, interest and profit.

The **economic agents** are **consumers**, **producers**, **service holders** and the **government**. A person can play more than one role.

key_terms.definition_md: Using goods and services to satisfy human wants.
Creating goods and services using land, labour, capital and enterprise.
Sharing the income from production among the factors that contributed.
A person who earns a salary or wage by working for others.

sections.heading: 5. Scope, functions and importance of statistics in economics
sections.body_md:
1. **Presents facts** in a precise, definite form.
2. **Condenses data** into summary measures such as averages and ratios.
3. **Finds relationships** between economic factors, such as price and quantity demanded, or income and saving.
4. **Forecasting** and **policy-making**, for example planning food stocks from past consumption.
5. Used by **consumers, producers, government and researchers**.

**Importance:** economic theories are tested with data, and policies are framed and judged with data.

sections.heading: 6. Limitations of statistics
sections.body_md:
1. It deals with **aggregates**, not single individuals.
2. Its results hold **on the average**, not in every case.
3. It can be **misused** if data are collected carelessly or interpreted wrongly.

These limits call for careful use; they do not make statistics useless.

key_terms.definition_md: A total or group of units taken together, as opposed to a single unit.

A result need not hold in every case

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Defining statistics in only one sense.
- Calling an attribute such as occupation quantitative.
- Confusing distribution (sharing the income of production) with the sale of goods.
- Writing a percentage without showing the formula.
- Saying an average holds for every individual.

**Tips**
- Use a specific example for every function.
- Mention aggregates and average truth when judging a claim.

questions.stem_md: Farida runs a bakery in the imagined town of Pipalnagar with one oven and ₹2,000 of daily raw material. She can bake only cakes or only bread in the oven during the morning shift. Which feature of the economic problem does her situation show?

options.text_md: Her wants are limited, so no choice is needed
Scarce resources have alternative uses, so a choice must be made
Resources are unlimited, so she can bake both without giving up anything
The choice is made by the government alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Scarce resources have alternative uses, so a choice must be made. One oven and a fixed sum of money can be put to different uses, so using them for cakes means giving up bread. This is scarcity with alternative uses, which forces a choice. Her resources are limited, not unlimited, and she herself decides what to bake.

questions.stem_md: Economics is best described as the study of

options.text_md: how to earn the highest possible profit in business
how governments collect taxes from citizens
how money is printed and circulated
how individuals and society choose to use scarce resources to satisfy wants

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** how individuals and society choose to use scarce resources to satisfy wants. The central idea of economics is choice under scarcity: wants are many, resources are limited, so people and societies must decide how to use them. Profit-making, taxation and printing money are only parts of what economics examines.

questions.stem_md: Neha buys a notebook and two pens from Gupta Stationers for her own use in school. In economic terms this activity is

options.text_md: consumption
production
distribution of income
government spending

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** consumption. Using goods and services to satisfy wants is consumption. Neha is the end user, so she is consuming. Production means creating goods or services, distribution means sharing output or income, and no government spending is involved.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined village of Karanpur, Raju turns timber, nails and labour into finished chairs in his workshop. This is an example of

options.text_md: consumption, because timber is being used up
distribution, because chairs will be sold later
production, because inputs are turned into goods that satisfy wants
saving, because he keeps the timber for later

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** production, because inputs are turned into goods that satisfy wants. Production is creating goods and services using inputs. Raju combines timber, nails and labour to make chairs. The timber is an input, not something a final user consumes, and selling the chairs would be a separate activity.

questions.stem_md: At the end of the month the owner of a tailoring unit in Sarangpur pays wages to the tailors, rent to the landlord of the shop and keeps the rest as profit. Which economic activity does this illustrate?

options.text_md: Consumption, since money is being spent
Production, since tailors are working
Distribution, since the earnings of production are shared among those who contributed
Forecasting, since profit is being planned

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Distribution, since the earnings of production are shared among those who contributed. The value created in production is divided as wages, rent, interest and profit among those who supplied labour, land, capital and enterprise; that sharing is distribution. The tailors working is production, and spending on goods later is consumption.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is regarded as an economic agent that provides public services such as roads and schools and collects taxes?

options.text_md: The government
A consumer
A producer of private goods
A service holder

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The government. The government undertakes public activities and raises revenue through taxes. A consumer uses goods, a producer makes goods for sale, and a service holder earns a salary or wage by working for others.

questions.stem_md: Imran works as a clerk in a cooperative bank in Rangpur and receives a monthly salary. In the classification of economic agents he is a

options.text_md: producer
government
consumer only
service holder

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** service holder. A service holder earns income by offering labour or skills for a salary or wage. He also consumes, but his role in earning is that of a service holder. He is not an owner producing goods for sale, and he is not the government.

questions.stem_md: Savitri owns a small unit that packs and sells spice mixes in Kanchanpur. She hires three workers and decides what to pack and at what price. Her role in the economy is mainly that of a

options.text_md: consumer
producer
service holder
regulator

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** producer. A producer organises inputs and creates goods or services for sale. Savitri hires workers and takes decisions on output and price. A consumer uses goods, a service holder works for a salary, and a regulator makes rules, which she does not.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about human wants and resources is correct?

options.text_md: Wants are unlimited, while the resources to satisfy them are limited
Wants are limited, while resources are unlimited
Both wants and resources are unlimited
Both wants and resources are limited, so choice never arises

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Wants are unlimited, while the resources to satisfy them are limited. People keep developing new wants as old ones are met, whereas land, labour, capital and time are limited. This gap is why choice is unavoidable. The other statements either reverse the idea or deny the problem.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Sarangpur panchayat office keeps a register of annual rainfall readings for six years: 820, 940, 760, 1,010, 880 and 870 millimetres. Used in this sense, the word statistics refers to

options.text_md: the science of collecting and analysing data
numerical facts, that is, data
a mathematical theory of chance
a way of drawing diagrams

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** numerical facts, that is, data. A collection of numerical facts is statistics in the plural sense. The science of collecting, organising and analysing them is statistics in the singular sense. Probability theory and diagrams are other topics.

questions.stem_md: Statistics used in the singular sense means

options.text_md: a set of numbers about one village
only the calculation of an average
the science of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting numerical data
the opinion of an expert about economic trends

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the science of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting numerical data. Statistics as a subject covers a whole chain of methods from collection to interpretation. A set of numbers is plural usage, an average is just one tool, and an expert opinion is not a statistical method.

questions.stem_md: A student says statistics is only about collecting numbers. Which reply is correct?

options.text_md: Correct, because analysis belongs to mathematics
Correct, because interpretation is left to the reader of the report
Wrong, because statistics only deals with analysis
Collection is only the first step; organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting follow

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Collection is only the first step; organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting follow. The subject covers all five stages, from collecting data to interpreting what the results mean. Saying it is only collection or only analysis leaves out parts of the process.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined survey of 80 households in Sarangpur, the surveyors note the main source of income of each household: farming, wage labour, trade, service or other. This information is

options.text_md: quantitative data, since it is measured in rupees
neither, since it is not numerical
quantitative, since there are five categories
qualitative data, which can be counted by category

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** qualitative data, which can be counted by category. The source of income is an attribute, not a measured amount, so the data are qualitative. After the households are sorted into categories, the number in each category can be counted. Having several categories does not make data quantitative.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an example of quantitative data?

options.text_md: Religion of each respondent in a survey
The preferred brand of tea of each customer
Monthly incomes of ten families in an imagined colony
Whether a student walks or cycles to school

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Monthly incomes of ten families in an imagined colony. Incomes are measured as numbers, so they are quantitative. Religion, brand preference and the way a student travels are attributes, hence qualitative.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined canteen survey of 60 students, 24 name tea as their favourite drink, 18 lassi, 12 juice and 6 coffee. Which statement about these data is most accurate?

options.text_md: The data are quantitative because drinks have prices
The favourite drink is a qualitative attribute; the counts 24, 18, 12 and 6 are numerical summaries of it
The counts are qualitative because they are about drinks
No numbers can be obtained from qualitative data

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The favourite drink is a qualitative attribute; the counts 24, 18, 12 and 6 are numerical summaries of it. What is recorded for each student, a drink, is an attribute. Counting how many fall in each category gives numbers that summarise it. Prices are not what was recorded, and attributes can always be counted by category.

questions.stem_md: Which function of statistics is shown when a report states that the average daily sale of Kavita Provision Store was ₹4,500 instead of listing every day's sale?

options.text_md: Condensing a mass of data into a summary measure
Forecasting
Testing a theory
Collecting primary data

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Condensing a mass of data into a summary measure. An average squeezes several readings into one figure that is easy to remember and compare. It does not predict the future, test a theory or collect new data.

questions.stem_md: An imagined bakery records that when the price of a bun is raised from ₹10 to ₹12, daily sales fall from 50 to 44 buns. Studying such pairs of figures helps economists to

options.text_md: present the data in a more attractive form only
find the relationship between price and quantity demanded
prove that all customers behave identically
decide who should be hired

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** find the relationship between price and quantity demanded. Putting two economic variables side by side shows how one changes when the other does, here the quantity demanded when price rises. The aim is not decoration, customers do not all behave alike, and hiring is a different matter.

questions.stem_md: The imagined town of Rangpur recorded monthly rice consumption of 400, 420, 440 and 460 tonnes in four successive years. An official uses this series to plan the food stock for the next year. Which use of statistics is this?

options.text_md: Defining a concept
Collecting data by a census
Classifying data by region
Forecasting and planning

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Forecasting and planning. The past trend is used to estimate a likely future requirement so that stocks can be arranged in time. That is forecasting for planning. The official is not collecting new data or classifying it.

questions.stem_md: A manufacturer of school bags in Kanchanpur studies sales figures from five towns to decide how many bags to make next season. This is an example of statistics being used by a

options.text_md: producer
consumer
researcher only
trade union

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** producer. The firm takes a decision on output from data on sales, so the user is a producer. A consumer would use data on prices or quality before a purchase, and the question does not describe research or a union.

questions.stem_md: Before buying a second-hand scooter, Harpreet notes the asking prices of seven similar scooters in her town and takes their average. Here statistics is helping a

options.text_md: producer, to fix output
government, to levy a tax
consumer, to judge a fair price
researcher, to publish a paper

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** consumer, to judge a fair price. Harpreet is a buyer using data to decide how much to pay, so she is acting as a consumer. No firm, tax or research report is involved.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT a function of statistics in economics?

options.text_md: Presenting economic facts in a precise and definite form
Helping to find relationships between economic factors
Guaranteeing that every individual in a group behaves like the group average
Supporting policy-making and forecasting

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Guaranteeing that every individual in a group behaves like the group average. Statistics summarises groups; it cannot ensure that each member matches the average. The other three are genuine functions.

questions.stem_md: Why are data important when economists test a theory such as the one linking income and saving?

options.text_md: Observed figures show whether the expected relationship actually holds
Data make the theory true by definition
Data are needed only to make the theory look complicated
Theories never need to be tested

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Observed figures show whether the expected relationship actually holds. A theory predicts how variables move together; real numbers let us check this prediction, and accept, change or reject the theory. Data cannot make a theory true by definition, and testing is essential.

questions.stem_md: A report says that the average monthly saving of the 5 imagined families of a lane is ₹5,400. Which limitation of statistics warns us against concluding that every family there saves ₹5,400?

options.text_md: Statistics is only a branch of mathematics
Statistics can be used only by the government
Statistics gives exact results always
Statistics deals with aggregates and not with single individuals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Statistics deals with aggregates and not with single individuals. The average describes the group as a whole; individual families may save much more or much less. The other statements are not limitations stated about this case.

questions.stem_md: A shop in Pipalnagar advertises that 9 out of 10 customers prefer its brand, but it asked only ten people standing at its own counter. What is the main problem with this claim?

options.text_md: Statistics can never be used in advertising
The data were collected carelessly, so the result may be misleading
Nine out of ten is not a possible ratio
Customers are not allowed to give opinions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The data were collected carelessly, so the result may be misleading. Ten people at the shop's own counter are not a fair picture of all customers, so the conclusion can mislead. This is the risk of misuse when data are collected or read carelessly. Statistics can be used in advertising when done properly.

questions.stem_md: Statistical laws are said to hold good on the average. Which situation best illustrates this?

options.text_md: In many lanes, higher-income families generally save more, though some higher-income family may save little
Every family with a higher income always saves more than every poorer family
No relation between income and saving can ever be found
A result found in one lane must be exactly true in every house

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** In many lanes, higher-income families generally save more, though some higher-income family may save little. Results of statistics describe a general tendency in a group, not an exact rule for every member. The other statements are either absolute or deny any pattern.

questions.stem_md: A district office compares the number of households in the imagined block of Rangpur with the number of ration shops before deciding where to open new ones. Statistics is here being used mainly for

options.text_md: testing a mathematical identity
policy-making and planning
advertising a product
defining a variable

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** policy-making and planning. Figures on households and shops guide where public facilities should go, which is planning and policy. No theory, advertisement or definition is involved.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Sarangpur village records annual rainfall of 820, 940, 760, 1,010, 880, 870 millimetres in six years. The average annual rainfall, as a summary measure of these data, is

options.text_md: 875 mm
880 mm
760 mm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 880 mm. The sum of the six readings is 5,280; divided by 6 this gives 880 mm. The median is 875 mm; the largest reading is 1,010 mm and the smallest is 760 mm, so these are not the average.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined survey of 80 households in Sarangpur, 32 households have farming as their main source of income. What percentage of the surveyed households is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 40%. Share = 32 ÷ 80 × 100 = 40%. The value 25% belongs to wage labour, 32 is a count and not a percentage, and 15% is the share of trade.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following lists names economic agents only?

options.text_md: Rainfall, income, price and saving
Census, survey, sample and questionnaire
Mean, median, mode and range
Consumers, producers, service holders and the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Consumers, producers, service holders and the government. Consumers, producers, service holders and the government are the agents who take economic decisions. The other lists name economic variables, methods of collecting data and summary measures.

questions.stem_md: A wheat farmer in Karanpur harvests 50 quintals, sells 30 quintals in the mandi, and keeps the remainder for his family's own food. For the wheat his family eats, which activity is taking place?

options.text_md: Production
Distribution
Consumption
Forecasting

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Consumption. Using wheat to meet the family's wants is consumption. The harvest itself was production, and the sale in the mandi belongs to the exchange and distribution chain.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Every society has to make choices about how to use its resources.

**Reason (R):** Human wants are unlimited, but the resources available to satisfy them are limited.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Because wants outrun resources, not every want can be met, which is exactly why choices must be made. So R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The word statistics is used in two senses.

**Reason (R):** Rainfall readings of six years can be shown in a bar chart.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but the second does not explain why the word has two senses: statistics means numerical facts in the plural sense and a science in the singular sense.

answer.model_answer_md: As **numerical data** (plural), statistics means collections of numerical facts, such as the rainfall readings of a village. As a **science** (singular), it is the method of **collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting** such data.

questions.stem_md: How does statistics help to present economic facts in a precise form? Give an imagined example.
questions.solution_md: Precision: exact numbers instead of vague statements.

answer.model_answer_md: Statistics replaces loose remarks with **exact figures**. Instead of saying the village had a good monsoon, a report can state that rainfall was **940 mm** in one year against **760 mm** in another, so the statement is definite and can be checked.

questions.stem_md: Kavita Provision Store sold goods worth ₹4,200, ₹3,800, ₹4,000, ₹4,600, ₹5,400, ₹5,000 on six days. How can statistics condense this series, and what does it give?
questions.solution_md: Average computed from the data; one figure replaces many.

answer.model_answer_md: The six sales can be summarised by an **average**: 27,000 ÷ 6 = **₹4,500** per day. One figure now stands for six, and it is easy to remember and to compare with other shops.

questions.stem_md: State any two limitations of statistics.
questions.solution_md: Any two of the usual limitations: aggregates, average truth, misuse.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Statistics deals with **aggregates**, not with single individuals, so it cannot describe one family exactly.
2. Its results are true **on the average**, so they need not hold in every particular case.

questions.stem_md: Give one imagined example each of how a producer and a consumer use statistics.
questions.solution_md: One decision based on data for each of the two users.

answer.model_answer_md: A **producer**, such as a Kanchanpur bag maker, studies past sales in different towns to decide next season's output. A **consumer**, such as a buyer of a second-hand scooter, compares the average of asking prices before bargaining.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by distribution as an economic activity? Illustrate with a small example from a workshop.
questions.solution_md: Define it as sharing of output value among factors; give wages, rent, profit.

answer.model_answer_md: **Distribution** is the sharing of the value produced among those who helped to produce it. In a workshop, the revenue from selling chairs is divided into **wages** for workers, **rent** for the shed owner and **profit** for the owner.

marking_scheme.step: Example with wages, rent and profit

questions.stem_md: Explain any three functions of statistics in economics.
questions.solution_md: Three of: presenting facts, condensing, relationships, forecasting, policy.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It **presents facts** in a precise and definite form through exact figures.
2. It **condenses data**: a mass of numbers is reduced to summary measures such as an average.
3. It helps to **find relationships**, for instance between price and quantity demanded, and supports **forecasting and policy-making**.

questions.stem_md: The imagined town of Rangpur had monthly rice consumption of 400, 420, 440, 460 tonnes in four successive years. Find the average yearly rise and the likely consumption in the fifth year if the trend continues. How is this forecast useful?
questions.solution_md: Average rise, projected figure, use for planning.

answer.model_answer_md: Total rise over the three gaps = 460 − 400 = 60; average yearly rise = 60 ÷ 3 = **20 tonnes**. Likely consumption next year = 460 + 20 = **480 tonnes**. The administration can arrange stocks and storage in advance to avoid shortage.

questions.stem_md: Why are data important for testing economic theories and for framing policies?
questions.solution_md: Testing theories, designing policy, evaluating it.

answer.model_answer_md: A **theory** says how variables should behave; **data** show whether they really do, so theories are retained, revised or dropped. For **policy**, data show the size of a problem such as food shortage and, later, whether the measure worked. Policy without data would rest on guesses.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between quantitative and qualitative data. Illustrate how qualitative data can still be summarised with numbers, using the imagined canteen survey of 60 students.
questions.solution_md: Definitions with examples, then counting by category with computed shares.

answer.model_answer_md: **Quantitative** data are measured numerically, such as marks or income. **Qualitative** data describe attributes, such as favourite drink. They cannot be measured, but they can be summarised by counting how many units fall in each category, and then finding the share of each. For example, of 60 students, 24 chose tea, which is 40%, and 18 chose lassi, which is 30%. In this way an attribute is turned into numbers that can be compared.

questions.stem_md: A newspaper in Pipalnagar reports that the average income of the town's families is ₹36,000 a month and concludes that no family there is poor. Comment with the help of the limitations of statistics.
questions.solution_md: Aggregates, average truth, wrong conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md: An **average** describes the whole town, not each family, since statistics deals with **aggregates**. Some families can earn far less than ₹36,000 while a few earn far more. So the conclusion is wrong; a result holding **on the average** cannot be applied to every family.

questions.stem_md: A pottery unit in the imagined village of Chandpur makes clay pots, pays wages and profit, and the pots are bought by households. Identify the three economic activities in this account and explain each briefly.
questions.solution_md: Production, distribution and consumption each tied to the passage.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Production:** the unit makes pots from clay and labour, which creates new goods that satisfy wants.
2. **Distribution:** the revenue from selling the pots is shared as wages for the potters and profit for the owner.
3. **Consumption:** households buy and use the pots to meet their wants. Each activity leads to the next: the pots made are sold, the revenue is shared, and the wages and profit are spent again on goods.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Dhillon family has a monthly income of ₹30,000 and spends ₹12,000 on food, ₹6,000 on rent, ₹3,000 on school and ₹5,000 on other items. Find the saving and the percentage of income spent on food.
questions.solution_md: Total spending, saving, food share.

answer.model_answer_md: Total spending = 12,000 + 6,000 + 3,000 + 5,000 = ₹26,000. Saving = 30,000 − 26,000 = **₹4,000**. Food share = 12,000 ÷ 30,000 × 100 = **40%**. So the family spends 40 per cent of its income on food and is able to save ₹4,000 each month after meeting all its planned expenses.

questions.stem_md: Explain why economics arises from scarcity and choice. Describe the three economic activities and the four economic agents.
questions.solution_md: Scarcity and choice, three activities, four agents.

answer.model_answer_md:
Human **wants are unlimited**, while **resources are scarce** and have alternative uses, so every individual and society must **choose**. Economics studies these choices.
The three economic activities are **consumption** (using goods to satisfy wants), **production** (creating goods and services) and **distribution** (sharing the income from production as wages, rent, interest and profit).
The four agents are **consumers**, who use goods; **producers**, who make goods for sale; **service holders**, who earn salaries or wages; and the **government**, which provides public services and raises taxes. Their decisions together decide how the scarce resources of the economy are used.

questions.stem_md: Explain the two senses in which the word statistics is used. Distinguish between quantitative and qualitative data with examples.
questions.solution_md: Two senses with examples, then the two kinds of data.

answer.model_answer_md:
In the **plural** sense, statistics means **numerical facts**, such as six years of village rainfall readings. In the **singular** sense, it is the **science** of **collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting** data.
**Quantitative** data are measured in numbers, for example income or marks. **Qualitative** data are attributes such as region or preference; they cannot be measured but can be **counted by categories**, for example how many chose tea.

questions.stem_md: Describe the scope and functions of statistics in economics, with an imagined example for at least three of them.
questions.solution_md: At least five functions or users; examples for three.

answer.model_answer_md: Statistics **presents facts precisely**, such as rainfall of 940 mm instead of heavy rain. It **condenses** many figures into a summary like an average sale. It helps to **find relationships**, for example price and quantity demanded of buns, or income and saving. It supports **forecasting**, such as planning rice stocks from four years of consumption, and **policy-making**. Consumers, producers, government and researchers all use it.

questions.stem_md: Examine the importance of statistics for economics. How do data help in testing economic theories and in framing and judging policies?
questions.solution_md: Theory testing, policy framing and evaluation, different users.

answer.model_answer_md: **Theories** state how economic variables should be related; **data** show whether the real world agrees, so a theory can be kept, changed or rejected. In **policy**, data measure the size of a problem such as shortage of food or jobs, help to choose measures, and later show whether the measure worked. Statistics also helps **consumers, producers and researchers** to decide with facts, and avoids decisions based on guesses.

questions.stem_md: Discuss the limitations of statistics. Do these limitations mean that statistics is useless? Give reasons.
questions.solution_md: Three limitations, then an evaluation that careful use keeps statistics valuable.

answer.model_answer_md: Statistics deals with **aggregates**, so it cannot describe a single family or person exactly. Its results are true **on the average** and may fail in a particular case. It can also be **misused** when data are collected from an unfair group or read carelessly. These limits do **not** make statistics useless: they warn us to use it with care. Properly collected data and correct reading give a sound basis for decisions in business and policy.

marking_scheme.step: Statement that statistics is not useless

questions.stem_md: In the imagined village of Chandpur, a weaving unit employs eight weavers, pays them wages, sells shawls to households and pays tax. Identify the activities and agents in this account and explain how statistics could help the unit.
questions.solution_md: Link each agent and activity to the passage; give a statistical use.

answer.model_answer_md: The unit is a **producer** and makes shawls: **production**. The eight weavers are **service holders** who receive wages, and the sharing of revenue as wages and profit is **distribution**. Households are **consumers** who buy shawls: **consumption**. The tax makes the **government** an agent. Statistics can help the owner by recording **sales** month by month, finding the **average** monthly sale to summarise them, comparing price with quantity sold to find the **relationship**, and **forecasting** demand for the next season so that enough yarn is bought in time.
